cards.front: How do combined strength, plyometric, and sprint training enhance neural drive and sprint performance?
cards.back:
Neural Drive: The rate and amplitude of action potential impulses transmitted from the central nervous system to target musculature.

Adaptations:
  • Strength Training: Increases the firing frequency (rate) and amplitude of impulses, directly enhancing muscular force production and the rate of force development (RFD).
  • Plyometric Training: Elevates the excitability of high-threshold motor neurons, which further amplifies neural drive and maximizes impulse generation during foot strike.

cards.front: What is the stretch–shortening cycle (SSC), and why is elite SSC performance considered independent of maximal strength?
cards.back:
Definition: An eccentric–concentric coupling phenomenon in which muscle–tendon complexes are rapidly and forcibly stretched (stretch-loaded) during an eccentric countermovement and immediately shortened in a reactive, elastic concentric contraction.

Independence from Strength: In elite athletic populations, reactive SSC capability relies on mechanical reflex loops and elastic strain energy storage rather than purely static, slow-velocity force generation, making SSC performance a distinct capability independent of 1RM maximal strength.

cards.tag: Dual Physiological Mechanisms of the SSC
cards.front: What two physiological phenomena are exploited during stretch–shortening cycle (SSC) actions?
cards.back:
1. Intrinsic Muscle–Tendon Behavior: Mechanical storage and recovery of elastic strain energy within muscle–tendon architecture (primarily the series elastic component/tendons).
  2. Reflex Feedback to the Nervous System: Rapid lengthening stimulates muscle spindle sensory organs, triggering a stretch-reflex response that provides force and length afferent feedback to augment concentric motor drive.

cards.tag: Acute vs. Chronic Adaptations to the SSC
cards.front: How do acute and chronic physiological adaptations to stretch–shortening cycle (SSC) actions differ?
cards.back:
• Acute Adaptations: Immediate elevation of mechanical efficiency and propulsive impulse through the instantaneous recovery of stored elastic strain energy.
  • Chronic Adaptations: Long-term morphological and neural remodeling that upregulates musculotendinous stiffness and enhances overall neuromuscular activation and motor unit synchronization.

cards.front: What two structural criteria must training fulfill to optimize SSC performance, and what is complex training?
cards.back:
Criteria for SSC Drills:
  1. Involve skillful, multijoint movements that transmit forces through the kinetic chain and exploit elastic–reflexive mechanisms.
  2. Structured around brief work bouts or clusters separated by frequent rest pauses to manage fatigue and prioritize technique.
Complex Training: Alternating heavy resistance exercises with biomechanically similar plyometric/SSC tasks within the same session to exploit postactivation potentiation (PAP), appropriate for advanced athletes but contraindicated for youths or novices.

cards.tag: Preactivation, Spindle Sensitivity, and Muscle Stiffness
cards.front: How do speed and strength training influence muscular preactivation prior to foot strike, and what is its physiological benefit?
cards.back:
Training increases preparatory preactivation (pre-tension) of lower limb muscles before ground contact.

Mechanism: Heightens the sensitivity of associated muscle spindles, which shortens the time required for sensory reflex feedback.

Benefit: Optimizes muscle stiffness and tendon compliance, establishing the foundational stiffness required to support the stretch–shortening cycle and prevent joint collapse under high impact loads.

cards.front: What is the spring–mass model (SMM), and how does it describe the mechanics of the stance phase in sprinting?
cards.back:
Definition: A mathematical model portraying sprinting as human locomotion where body mass displacement is driven by the collective compression and recoil of spring-like muscle-tendon structures.

Stance Phase Dynamics:
  • Initial Foot Strike: Compression of the leg spring begins, absorbing force and producing brief horizontal braking forces that help propel the opposite swing leg forward.
  • Midstance: Lowest vertical point of the center of mass, corresponding to maximal spring compression.
  • Push-Off: Rapid return of stored elastic energy through spring extension, projecting the sprinter forward into flight.

cards.tag: Elite vs. Non-Elite Stance Phase Kinetics
cards.front: How do elite sprinters deviate from the classic spring–mass model (SMM) during maximal-velocity sprinting compared to non-elite athletes?
cards.back:
• Non-Elite Athletes (Field/Team Sports): Display stance phases that closely adhere to the classic SMM, generating a relatively symmetrical vertical force curve across ground contact.
  • Elite Sprinters: Deviate from the classic model by producing an asymmetrical vertical force curve, generating the vast majority of their vertical force in the first half of ground contact to rapidly reverse downward velocity.
Note: As stride frequency increases at a given running speed, increasing leg spring stiffness is paramount.

cards.front: How do typical ground contact times compare across maximal-velocity sprinting, acceleration, agility, and change-of-direction maneuvers?
cards.back:
Ground contact times follow a distinct continuum:
  • Maximal-Velocity Sprinting: 0.09 to 0.11 seconds (ultra-short, fast SSC).
  • Sprint Acceleration Phase: 0.17 to 0.20 seconds.
  • Agility Plant Phase: 0.23 to 0.25 seconds.
  • Change-of-Direction (COD) Plant Phase: 0.44 to 0.722 seconds (extended, long SSC).
Because COD and agility plant phases are substantially longer, they rely on long-duration SSC actions and heavy eccentric braking.

cards.front: Why is high-velocity eccentric training essential for agility braking, and how do tactical scenarios alter agility neurophysiology?
cards.back:
Eccentric Specialization: Effective braking requires specialized eccentric training because:
  1. Motor unit recruitment pathways during eccentric muscle actions differ from those used in concentric contractions.
  2. Neuromuscular adaptations to eccentric loading are velocity-specific.
Perceptual–Cognitive Integration: Agility neurophysiology extends beyond mechanical braking into visual scanning, anticipation, and decision-making; the brain processing strategy shifts fundamentally depending on whether the athlete is in an offensive vs. defensive tactical scenario.
